quote: The way the current program is set up is there is no out of pocket cost or any upfront fees. All we're doing is we call the bill swap to our swapping what you're currently paying with your electricity company to a less than silver rate.
stewart_read: This line is garbled ('less than silver rate') and front-loads program mechanics before any qualification has happened, and the customer immediately says she didn't understand any of it. This is a delivery/clarity failure, not a strategic choice.
alternative_hypothesis: Could be read as the rep trying to quickly answer her ZIP-code/government-program question, but the content given doesn't actually answer that question at all.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to slow down and use plain language on the bill-swap concept, and to directly answer the customer's actual question (ZIP code / government program) before reciting the standard pitch.

quote: if, I I wanted to find out if I was in the ZIP code that the government is paying for this.
stewart_read: Customer opens with a misconception (government paying for solar via ZIP code) that the rep never directly corrects or addresses — he pivots straight to the bill-swap pitch without clarifying what the program actually is or isn't.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may have believed his general program explanation implicitly answered this, but the customer's confusion at 00:59 suggests it did not land as an answer to her specific question.
coaching_implication: Rep should directly name and correct the misconception ('this isn't a government payment program, here's what it actually is') before moving into verify — leaving it unaddressed risks the customer carrying a false frame into any future appointment.

quote: The one big one's not k. Towards the street, towards the side of that. You're looking at the house. I had that big monster taken out.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers that a large shading tree was removed roughly four months ago — a sun-exposure improvement signal that increases solar viability. Rep does capture the timing but doesn't use it to build excitement about improved production potential.
coaching_implication: Rep correctly logged the detail for imagery-update purposes, but could have reflected it back as a positive ('great, that opens up your roof to a lot more sun') to build momentum rather than treating it as a pure data point.

stewart_read: Bill figure is garbled in the transcript but clearly in a high range given the follow-up conversation about $250-500/month; rep captured it and asked a decent follow-up ('has it kind of always been that high') but never got to flip it into an emotional alignment-against-utility because the call ended on the credit DQ.
coaching_implication: This is a capture-without-flip case cut short by the DQ — not a rep failure to flip so much as the call ending before the flip could happen. Still worth noting for pattern-tracking across calls.

quote: and it's running over shit, 4 or 500.
stewart_read: Customer reveals her grandson's family is now living in a mobile/'noble' home on the property, adding a second household's electric usage on top of her own bill — a significant usage-increase signal that strengthens the case for a larger system.
coaching_implication: Rep should have flagged this as a notable usage driver worth mentioning in a design/follow-up note; it materially changes the sizing conversation and is exactly the kind of detail a closer would want to know if this lead is revisited in a couple months.

quote: Is that gonna be an issue for you at all?
stewart_read: Rep asks the credit qualifier directly per script, which is correct procedure, but per Spencer's operator note in the schema, DQ'ing on a self-reported estimate ('about 650, I believe') rather than routing to an actual credit pull may be killing a viable deal on unreliable self-report.
alternative_hypothesis: If Ion's policy is that setters must DQ on stated credit, this is correct procedure, not a failure.
coaching_implication: Flag for manager: this is the open policy question in qualifiers.credit_qualifier — until Kenny resolves whether setters DQ on stated number or pass everyone to the closer's pull, this exact moment (self-reported 'about 650, I believe') is a coachable judgment call worth discussing.

quote: Unfortunately, then at the moment, it wouldn't really make sense.
stewart_read: The customer had just described a rising, already-high bill made worse by a second household drawing power — exactly the situation the objection_inversion pattern is built for (the financial pain that justifies solar is being treated as the reason to disqualify). Rep accepts the credit answer at face value and closes the door without probing the estimate or offering any alternative financing path.
alternative_hypothesis: Rep may be strictly following a hard DQ rule if Ion's policy requires setters to DQ on stated credit below 670 with no exceptions, in which case this is correct procedure, not a miss.
coaching_implication: Regardless of the policy answer, the rep never asked whether she was estimating or certain, and never mentioned alternative purchase options without the tax credit or financing paths for near-threshold credit — a probe that costs nothing and could preserve the lead.

quote: I'll get it notated down here to just follow-up with you in a couple months, but, yeah, I didn't wanna waste your time going through all the weeds and everything like that.
stewart_read: The call ends with a vague future follow-up ('a couple months') with no specific date, no handshake confirmation, and no text-follow-up promise — this is a procedurally soft close even for a DQ'd lead.
coaching_implication: Even on a DQ, coach the rep to give a concrete next-touch commitment (e.g., 'I'll reach back out the week of [month]') rather than an open-ended 'couple months,' so the lead doesn't go cold with no trigger to reopen it.
